name: DATABASE
description: The database (D) functions are a family of Excel and Google Sheets functions that perform calculations on records in a list or database that satisfy one or more conditions. They all share the same three-argument signature: a database range, a field, and a criteria range.
tldr: D-functions calculate on database rows that match a criteria range, using a shared (database, field, criteria) signature.

parameters.name: database
parameters.description: The range of cells that makes up the list or database, including the header row as its first row. Each column is a field and each following row is a record.

parameters.name: field
parameters.description: The column to use in the calculation. Supply the column label in quotes (e.g. "Yield") or the column's 1-based position within the database (e.g. 4).

parameters.name: criteria
parameters.description: The range of cells that contains the conditions, including a header row that matches database column names and at least one condition row beneath it. A record matches only if it satisfies every condition in a given criteria row; multiple criteria rows are treated as OR.

basicExample.description: Sum the Yield of apple trees taller than 10 using the shared D-function pattern
basicExample.explanation: The criteria range A9:B10 holds Tree = Apple and Height > 10; only two records match (Yield 14 and 10), which sum to 24.

advancedExamples.title: How the criteria range works
advancedExamples.description: The database is A1:E7 with headers Tree, Height, Age, Yield, Profit. The criteria block A9:B10 reuses two of those headers so the function knows which columns to filter on.
advancedExamples.explanation: Matching rows have Yield 14 and 10, so the average is (14+10)/2 = 12. The criteria headers must exactly match database headers for the filter to apply.

advancedExamples.title: Multiple criteria rows act as OR
advancedExamples.scenario: Find tall apples OR any cherry tree
advancedExamples.description: Build a criteria range with two condition rows: row one is Tree=Apple, Height>10; row two is Tree=Cherry. Records matching either row are included.
advancedExamples.explanation: Two tall apples plus the single cherry record match, giving a count of 3 numeric Yield values.

howItWorks: Each D-function first filters the database rows so that only records matching the criteria range remain. It then applies its specific calculation (sum, average, count, max, min, product, or a statistic) to the values in the specified field column of those matching records. Filtering uses the same rules as Excel's advanced filter: criteria on the same row are AND-ed, criteria on different rows are OR-ed, and operators such as >, <, >=, <=, <>, and wildcards (*, ?) are supported.

howToSteps.name: Build the database
howToSteps.text: Put your data in a range with a header row of unique column names, one record per row.

howToSteps.name: Build the criteria range
howToSteps.text: Copy the column header(s) you want to filter on to a separate area and type the condition(s) below them.

howToSteps.name: Write the D-function
howToSteps.text: Call =DFUNC(database, "Field", criteria) with the field name in quotes or its column index.

limitations: The criteria header labels must exactly match the database headers or the condition is ignored.
Field names with spaces or special characters must be quoted; an unquoted bare column name in the formula will error.
DCOUNT only counts numeric cells, while DCOUNTA counts any non-blank cell, so they can return different results.

commonErrors.cause: The field argument is a text column name not enclosed in quotes, or the criteria range has no header.
commonErrors.fix: Wrap the field name in double quotes and ensure the criteria range includes a header row.

commonErrors.cause: Criteria headers do not match database headers, so no rows are filtered.
commonErrors.fix: Make the criteria header text identical to the database column name.

googleSheetsEquivalent.description: Google Sheets supports all the same D-functions with identical syntax and behavior.
googleSheetsEquivalent.notes: Criteria and wildcard rules match Excel exactly.

faq.question: What is the difference between field as text and as a number?
faq.answer: You may pass the column label in quotes, e.g. "Yield", or its 1-based position, e.g. 4. Both refer to the same column.

faq.question: How do I filter on more than one column?
faq.answer: Add more condition columns to the criteria range, each with a matching header. Conditions on the same row are AND-ed; additional rows are OR-ed.

faq.question: Which D-function should I use to count matches?
faq.answer: Use DCOUNT to count numeric matches and DCOUNTA to count any non-blank matches; use DGET to pull a single value when exactly one record matches.
